newsitem.title: SYRIA: Luxembourg says time ripe for Syria-Israel talks.
newsitem.headline: Luxembourg says time ripe for Syria-Israel talks.

text.p: Luxembourg's Foreign Minister Jacques Poos said on Thursday the deal between Israel and the Palestinians over the West Bank town of Hebron would help pave the way for resumption of Syrian-Israeli peace talks.
"This deal will pave the way for work to solve other issues regarding the resumption of Israel's peace talks with both Syria and Lebanon," Poos said.
Speaking to Reuters before opening talks with his Syrian counterpart Farouq Al-Shara at the Syrian foreign ministry in Damascus, Poos said:
"The Hebron deal is a positive step on the way to peace in the Middle East which we hope will be fully implemented and honoured by both parties..."
Israel and the Palestinians, concluding months of talks on Israeli forces' partial withdrawal from Hebron, signed the deal early on Wednesday.
Poos said his discussions with Shara would focuss on how to reactivate Syria's peace talks with Israel and what Luxembourg and the European Union could do in this respect.
The Luxembourg minister arrived in Damascus on Wednesday on a Middle East tour that has also taken him to Israel, the Palestinian self-ruled areas, Cairo, and Amman.
He will leave later on Thursday for Lebanon for similar talks with Lebanese leaders before returning home.
Poos said his tour of the region was in preparation for his country's takeover of the European Union's rotating presidency later this year.
Asked about the prospects of war between Syria and Israel after bellicose statements made recently by both states, Poos said:

"I did not feel any threat of war between Syria and Israel during my talks in Israel... on the contrary I felt there was keen interest by Israeli officials to resume peace talks with Syria and before anything else to resume contacts with Damascus."

Syria has accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of working to undermine the peace process when he rejected an agreement to swap occupied Arab lands for peace, a principle on which Arab-Israeli peace talks were launched in Madrid in 1991.
Damascus said the negotiations, suspended since Netanyahu took office in June last year, would not resume until he accepts full Israeli withdrawal from the Golan Heights, captured from Syria in 1967.
"We wanted to have direct contacts with all players in the Middle East peace process to prepare ourselves to be in a better position to offer any help when needed," Poos said.
